candidates.attacker_control: The values are fully attacker-controlled: `emails[*]` in the JSON body of `POST /invite_users` (`InvitationsEndpoint.inviteUsers` @RequestBody InvitationsRequest), `newEmail` in the change-email flow, `email` in `/email_verifications`, the signup email in `EmailAccountCreationService`, and the authenticated username string in `UaaChangePasswordService`. For the strongest instance the request also carries an attacker-chosen `redirect_uri` and optional `client_id` (both request parameters), and the caller needs a bearer token with `scim.invite` (or a zone-admin/zone-scoped token), per uaa/src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/spring/login-ui.xml `/invite_users/**` rule.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that SQL values are bound as parameters (SimpleSearchQueryConverter.comparisonClause, AbstractQueryable.query), so this is filter-semantics injection, not SQL injection; the existing sqlInjectionAttack* tests therefore pass. Verified the SCIM parser accepts an unparenthesized `or` (SimpleSearchQueryConverterTests.invalid_conditional_or expects the [or]-handling message, not a parse error). Verified attribute whitelisting accepts email/origin/identity_zone_id. Verified the endpoint's email regex is permissive enough to admit the payload while the `invite_User_With_Invalid_Emails` test only rejects clearly malformed addresses. Verified the takeover step does not require the old password (EmailInvitationsService line 68, JdbcScimUserProvisioning.changePassword lines 281-283). Noted and weighed the mitigating factors: only unverified accounts can be taken over (verified users are auto-accepted with an empty password); the actor must already hold scim.invite/zone-admin (zone admins can also reset users' passwords via PUT /Users/{id}/password, so for them this is not an escalation); the `EmailAccountCreationService` instance is not exploitable because its catch path requires a duplicate-username failure first; the `UaaChangePasswordService` instance still requires the target's current password; the escaping in UaaResetPasswordService shows the project's own mitigation pattern and the unused UaaStringUtils.toJsonString suggests a reverted usage, but I could not prove which call site a fix targeted. No runtime testing was performed; the exploit chain is a source-level hypothesis, not a confirmed exploit.
candidates.impact: Privilege boundary violation and account takeover: a caller whose only intended right is to invite new users (`scim.invite`) can, by manipulating the invited address, cause UAA to issue and disclose a valid invitation/registration secret for another pre-existing user in the zone (including roles that user holds, e.g. administrators of that zone) and then set that user's password without knowing the old one. It additionally leaks the victim's user id/primary email and lets the attacker mark the account verified. The same unescaped-filter pattern in the sibling locations lets values alter lookup semantics (e.g. email-change duplicate checks, change-password user lookup), where the impact is bounded by additional checks (see counterevidence).
candidates.prerequisites: 1) A caller authenticated as a client/user that holds `scim.invite` or `zones.{zone.id}.admin` (login-ui.xml, invitationsEndpointSecurity). 2) The zone must resolve the injected address to exactly one active identity provider (default single-provider zone does; DomainFilter wildcard checks accept a two-dot domain string such as `evil.com" or email eq "victim@example.com`). 3) The injected filter must be accepted by the SCIM parser — proven feasible at the syntax level by SimpleSearchQueryConverterTests.invalid_conditional_or, which shows `A eq "x" or B eq "y"` parses and reaches the [or]-handling code. 4) The target's email must exist in the same zone with origin `uaa`, and the attacker's own address must not match an existing user (otherwise the result is >1 → ScimResourceConflictException). 5) For the takeover step, the target account must not yet be verified: for a verified user, the GET accept handler calls acceptInvitation(code, "") and no password is set. 6) The final old-password-free change relies on EmailInvitationsService.acceptInvitation passing a null old password, which JdbcScimUserProvisioning.changePassword only checks when non-null.
candidates.root_cause: User-controlled values are concatenated raw into SCIM filter strings that are parsed and converted into SQL WHERE clauses. In `InvitationsEndpoint.findOrCreateUser` the invited address is interpolated as `String.format("email eq \"%s\" and origin eq \"%s\"", email, origin)` (line 140). A value such as `attacker@evil.com" or email eq "victim@example.com` passes the endpoint's loose `^(.+)@(.+)\.(.+)$` check and the domain filter, and turns the lookup into `email eq "attacker@evil.com" or (email eq "victim@example.com" and origin eq "uaa")`, so the query can return the victim's ScimUser instead of the inviter. The endpoint then mints an INVITATION expiring code for that user's `user_id` and returns the invitation link (`inviteLink`) in the `new_invites` response; redeeming it via `/invitations/accept(.do)` calls `EmailInvitationsService.acceptInvitation` → `scimUserProvisioning.changePassword(userId, null, password, zone)` (old password not required) and marks the account verified. The project already treats this input class as a risk elsewhere: `UaaResetPasswordService.forgotPassword` escapes the email with `JsonUtils.writeValueAsString(email)` (line 157) and the helper `UaaStringUtils.toJsonString` (model, lines 283-289) exists for exactly this purpose but has no callers in main code — the same unescaped pattern remains in several sibling classes (locations below).
candidates.title: SCIM filter injection through unescaped user input (invitation lookup returns and leaks another user's invitation code → account takeover)
candidates.trace: POST /invite_users (body {"emails":["attacker@evil.com\" or email eq \"victim@example.com"]}) → InvitationsEndpoint.inviteUsers (email regex matches) → DomainFilter.filter returns the single UAA provider → findOrCreateUser(email, "uaa") (line 138) → users.query(...) with the injected filter → AbstractQueryable.query wraps it as "(<filter>) and identity_zone_id eq \"<zone>\"" (lines 75-82) → SimpleSearchQueryConverter.convert/scimFilter (SCIMFilter.parse succeeds, attributes email/origin/identity_zone_id are whitelisted) → createFilter builds "(LOWER(email)=:p0 OR LOWER(email)=:p1 AND LOWER(origin)=:p2)" with bound parameters (no SQL injection) → the row for the victim is returned → InvitationsEndpoint mints an INVITATION ExpiringCode containing the victim's user_id/email (lines 105-117) and returns `inviteLink` to the caller → attacker GETs /invitations/accept?code=... (InvitationsController.acceptInvitePage renders the accept page for the unverified victim) → POST /invitations/accept.do with a chosen password → EmailInvitationsService.acceptInvitation → scimUserProvisioning.changePassword(victimUserId, null, password, zone) → attacker authenticates as the victim.
candidates.unverified: The exact SCIM grammar acceptance of the composite payload (quotes plus `or` mixed with the trailing `and`) is inferred from parser unit tests, not executed; the domain-filter/DomainFilter outcome for the crafted address is reasoned from wildcard patterns, not executed; whether a deployment's clients commonly hold `scim.invite`, and whether a real target account is unverified, are deployment-dependent; I did not demonstrate the final password change end-to-end and did not confirm this is the specific benchmark vulnerability — it is the strongest source-evidenced lead I could establish within the read-only constraints.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-943/CWE-90-style improper neutralization of special elements in a query/filter (SCIM filter injection)

coverage_summary: Source scope reported 1447 root files / 1446 model-visible files after the tool's safety filters (1 file excluded for a sensitive name or path; no files excluded for size; binaries with NUL bytes in the first 8 KiB are refused/skipped, and symlinks are not followed). P1 relation scope: index status "partial", 1063 Java files parsed with 0 parse errors and 116 files omitted from the index; the index provides only syntax containment plus name/type/arity-based call and inheritance candidates, with no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution, Spring DI/security enforcement, runtime reachability, or exploitability analysis, and 74366 unresolved calls — so index records were used only for navigation and every candidate was verified against source text. I inspected the security-relevant paths in the Java source (server, model, uaa test/config XML, resources) listed in the summary plus the Spring security XMLs, the SCIM filter/SQL pipeline, account and invitation flows, zone switching and zone resolution, LDAP/SAML/OIDC provider code, and the CORS/CSRF/header filters. I did not review in depth: client-lib and sample modules (beyond token request helpers), most of the 4258-line TokenMvcMockTests and other large integration suites, UaaTokenServices internals in full, the SAML/IdP metadata generators in full, Thymeleaf templates, JavaScript/CSS assets, DB migration SQL, and the ~116 index-omitted files; no build, test, scanner, or runtime execution was performed.
limitations: The candidate is a lead derived from source reading only; no exploit was executed and no runtime reachability was proven (no code execution, no tests, no scanners).

The SCIM filter injection depends on the unboundid SCIMFilter parser accepting the composite injected filter and on the zone's provider/domain configuration; I verified the parser accepts a top-level `or` only indirectly, via an existing unit test expectation.

Impact for the strongest instance is limited to accounts that are not yet verified (verified users' invitations are accepted with an empty password), and the actor must already hold `scim.invite` or zone-admin scope; for zone admins this is not an escalation over their existing ability to change passwords in the zone.

Regarding the same root cause at the other listed sites, the change-email/change-password/account-creation instances appear to be guarded by additional checks (conflict check only, current-password check, duplicate-creation precondition), so their demonstrable impact is lower.

The P1 relation index is partial (116 omitted files, no data flow / reachability), so absence of an indexed edge is not evidence of absence; unreviewed areas listed in the coverage summary remain unexamined.
The presence of one excluded sensitive file/path and the exclusion of binary-like files means a small part of the tree could not be inspected at all.

Whether this matches the benchmark's ground-truth vulnerability is unverified; the open-redirect and other leads above were considered and rejected only on the strength of the source evidence available in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Post-login open redirect via the `form_redirect_uri` request parameter (UaaSavedRequestAwareAuthenticationSuccessHandler.determineTargetUrl lines 34-46, plus UaaSavedRequestCache lines 55-96).
rejected_leads.reason: The handler returns the raw parameter, but the repository's own tests assert this behavior as intended (UaaSavedRequestAwareAuthenticationSuccessHandlerTests.form_parameter_works expects http://test.com; TokenMvcMockTests.test_authorization_code_grant_redirect_when_session_expires expects a 302 to the posted form value), and delivering an attacker value to a victim requires a CSRF-protected POST to /login.do, so no concrete attacker-controlled trust-boundary crossing could be established. Left as an unconfirmed lead, not a candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Pre-authentication open redirect via the unvalidated `redirect_uri` of the saved request in LoginSAMLAuthenticationFailureHandler.onAuthenticationFailure (lines 34-57).
rejected_leads.reason: The value is taken from the session saved request and appended to an error URL without checking the client's registered redirect URIs, but exploitation requires a failed SAML login interaction for the victim and there is no counter-check helper being bypassed in the snapshot; weaker and less certain than the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: `AccessController.getRedirectUri` returns `clientAuth.getRedirectUri()` with a `//TODO - SHOULD WE ALLOW THIS??` comment (lines 258-276).
rejected_leads.reason: By the time this controller renders the consent page, UaaAuthorizationEndpoint (lines 172-193) has already resolved/validated the redirect via AntPathRedirectResolver, so the value in the session AuthorizationRequest is the validated one.

rejected_leads.lead: `PasswordChangeEndpoint.checkPasswordChangeIsAllowed` returns immediately for client-only callers (lines 124-128), letting a client with `password.write` change any user's password without the old one.
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented purpose of the privileged `password.write` scope and is consistent with the security XML; no deviation from the design could be shown.

rejected_leads.lead: `/email_verifications` + `/email_changes` (ChangeEmailEndpoints) accept an arbitrary userId and return the EMAIL code to the caller, and `/password_*` returns password-reset codes to callers with `oauth.login`/zone-admin scope (PasswordResetEndpoint lines 73-96).
rejected_leads.reason: Both endpoint groups are gated to trusted login-server (`oauth.login`) or zone-admin callers by spring/login-ui.xml and login-server-security.xml; the behavior follows from those trust assumptions rather than from a missing check.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in `validateXml` of SamlIdentityProviderDefinition/SamlServiceProviderDefinition (setExpandEntityReferences(false) without disabling external entities).
rejected_leads.reason: Both methods reject any metadata containing `<!DOCTYPE` before parsing, which blocks the usual XXE vectors; no bypass was found.

rejected_leads.lead: `ScimGroupEndpoints.getGroupId` injects the path-variable displayName into `displayName eq "..."` (line 332) and `AccessController.getScopes` injects the requested scope into a group lookup (line 231).
rejected_leads.reason: Same filter-injection root cause as the submitted candidate but with much weaker impact (external-group mapping manipulation of a group selected by name; group description displayed on the consent page), so they are mentioned as part of the same root cause rather than as separate candidates.

summary: Reviewed the Cloud Foundry UAA snapshot (gradle.properties version 4.5.5-SNAPSHOT) with the same source filters for B0/P1. Broader review covered the OAuth/token stack (UaaAuthorizationEndpoint, AntPathRedirectResolver, UaaTokenServices-adjacent classes, TokenRevocationEndpoint, CheckTokenEndpoint, OnboardingChecks), SCIM/user provisioning and SCIM filter → SQL conversion (SimpleSearchQueryConverter, AbstractQueryable, JdbcScimUserProvisioning, JdbcScimGroupProvisioning), account flows (password reset, change-password, invitations, email change/creation), zone handling (IdentityZoneSwitchingFilter, IdentityZoneEndpoints, ZoneManagementScopes), LDAP/SAML/OIDC provider code, CORS/CSRF/header filters, and the Spring security XML. The single strongest source-evidenced candidate is SCIM-filter injection caused by unescaped values concatenated into SCIM filter strings, with the invitation lookup as the most damaging instance: a caller holding the `scim.invite` scope (or `zones.<id>.admin`) can inject SCIM operators through the invited email so the lookup returns a different, pre-existing user, obtain that user's INVITATION code in the HTTP response, and then redeem it to set that user's password (account takeover). Other files share the same root cause and are listed as locations; several other suspicious areas were checked and rejected as unconfirmed leads.
